demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 52-year-old South Asian man who presents for an initial evaluation at the urging of his adult daughter. He is a thin, soft-spoken man who sits hunched forward in his chair, his hands resting motionless on his knees. He struggles to make eye contact and speaks in a low, careful voice, as if afraid of being overheard.

The event that changed everything happened fourteen months ago. Mr. A. works as a cleaner for a commercial office building, a job he has held for nearly a decade. He takes pride in his work, arriving before dawn to vacuum, mop, and empty trash bins before the first employees arrive. On that morning, he was pushing a heavy industrial cart loaded with cleaning supplies and a full trash bag down a long, dimly lit hallway. He did not see the woman. She was an elderly office worker, a woman he knew by sight, someone who always smiled and said good morning. She had stepped out of a side corridor, and the cart struck her. The impact knocked her backward. She fell, her head hitting the corner of a marble planter. Mr. A. remembers the sound—a wet, hollow thud. He remembers the blood spreading on the floor before he could even kneel down. He remembers her eyes, wide and blank, and then the screaming. He called 911, but by the time paramedics arrived, she was unresponsive. She survived, but with a severe traumatic brain injury. She now requires round-the-clock care and has not regained full consciousness.

In the days and weeks that followed, Mr. A. could not stop replaying the scene. He would be standing at a sink, washing dishes, and suddenly he would see her face, the angle of her neck, the blood. He would feel the impact in his own hands. He stopped sleeping. When he did fall asleep, he would jerk awake, heart pounding, convinced he had just hit someone again. He stopped taking the bus, because the sudden stops and starts made him flinch. He stopped going to the temple, because the chanting and the incense made him feel dizzy and trapped.

His work became unbearable. He requested a transfer to a different building, but the new location had the same long hallways, the same dim corners. He now walks with his back to the wall, constantly scanning the floor for shadows. He flinches when a coworker approaches from behind. He has started arriving two hours early, just to have the building empty. His supervisor has noticed his slow pace, his frequent breaks, his refusal to use the cart. He has been given a written warning for “inefficiency.”

At home, Mr. A. lives alone in a small apartment. His wife left him three years ago, before the accident, citing his emotional distance. He has not spoken to her since. His daughter calls every week, but he often lets the call go to voicemail. He does not know what to say. He feels a constant, low-grade shame, a sense that he is a dangerous person, that he should not be around others. He avoids crowded places—grocery stores, markets, family gatherings. He has not visited his mother, who lives two hours away, because he is afraid he will cause another accident.

He describes his mood as “flat.” He has lost interest in cooking, in watching cricket, in reading the newspaper. He spends most of his time sitting on his couch, staring at the television without seeing it. He has started drinking three or four beers every evening, not to feel better, but to feel less. He has not told his daughter about the drinking. He has not told anyone about the nightmares, which have become more vivid. In the most recent one, he is pushing the cart, but the hallway is filled with people, and he cannot stop. He wakes up gasping, covered in sweat, and does not go back to sleep.

He says he does not deserve to feel better. He says he should have been more careful. He says he thinks about the woman’s family every day. He does not cry when he says this. His face remains still, as if the emotion has been locked somewhere deep inside.
